knowledge_point.title: Evaluating the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Using a Substitution

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+(t+1)\,j\,$ for $t\in [\sqrt{2},\sqrt{6}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(t^{2})\,i+(t + 1)\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=t^{2}$, $y=t + 1$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t + 1)\,j \\  & =(2 t)\,i+(1)\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2 t)^2+(1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{12 x}{y - 1}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{12(t^{2})}{(t + 1)-(1)} \\  & =\frac{12t^2}{t} \\  & =12 t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}(12 t)(\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4 t^{2} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(8 t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{3}{2}\cdot u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{9}^{25} \\  & =1[(25)^{3/2}-(9)^{3/2}] \\  & =1[(125)-(27)] \\  & =(125)-(27) \\  & =98\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)=3t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j\,$ for $t\in [0,1].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(3 t)\,i+(t^{3})\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=3 t$, $y=t^{3}$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{3})\,j \\  & =(3)\,i+(3 t^{2})\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(3)^2+(3 t^{2})^2} \\  & =\sqrt{9 t^{4} + 9} \\  & =3 \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x^{3} + y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3 t)^3+(1)(t^{3}) \\  & =27t^3+1t^3 \\  & =28 t^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(28 t^{3})(3 \sqrt{t^{4} + 1})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}84 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=t^{4} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(4 t^{3})\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{1}^{2}21\cdot u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =21\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{1}^{2} \\  & =14[(2)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =14[(2 \sqrt{2})-(1)] \\  & =(28 \sqrt{2})-(14) \\  & =-14 + 28 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$  along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i-{t}^{2}\,j$ for $0<t<\sqrt{\pi /2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(t^{2})\,i+(- t^{2})\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=t^{2}$, $y=- t^{2}$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t^{2})\,j \\  & =(2 t)\,i+(- 2 t)\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2 t)^2+(- 2 t)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{8 t^{2}} \\  & =2 \sqrt{2}|t| \\  & =2 \sqrt{2} t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ because $t\geq0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\cos{\left(x \right)}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\cos{\left(t^{2} \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}}(\cos{\left(t^{2} \right)})(2 \sqrt{2} t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=t^{2}$, $\text{d}u=(2 t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{2}\cdot \cos u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\sin u\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-\sin(0)] \\  & =\sqrt{2}[(1)-(0)] \\  & =(\sqrt{2})-(0) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5},$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(4 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=4 \sin{\left(t \right)}$, $y=- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j \\  & =(4 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(4 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2+(- 3 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2} \\  & =\sqrt{16\cos^2 t+9\cos^2 t} \\  & =\sqrt{25 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}} \\  & =5|\cos t| \\  & =5 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\cos t|=\cos t$ because $\cos t\geq0$ along this interval.

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{x^{2}}{5} + \frac{y^{2}}{5}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(4 \sin{\left(t \right)})^2+(- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)})^2}{5} \\  & =\frac{16\sin^2 t+9\sin^2 t}{5} \\  & =5 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(5 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)})(5 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}25 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\sin{\left(t \right)}$, $\text{d}u=(\cos{\left(t \right)})\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{0}^{1}25\cdot u^2\,\text{d}u \\  & =25\cdot\frac{u^3}{3}\big|_{0}^{1} \\  & =25[\frac{(1)^3}{3}-\frac{(0)^3}{3}] \\  & =25[\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-(0)] \\  & =\left(\frac{25}{3}\right)-(0) \\  & =\frac{25}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $$
\displaystyle r(t)=t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,k
$$
for $1<t<\sqrt{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(t)\,i+\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right)\,j+\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right)\,k$, then along the curve we have $x=t$, $y=\frac{t^{2}}{2}$, $z=\frac{t^{2}}{2}$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right)\,k \\  & =(1)\,i+(t)\,j+(t)\,k \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(1)^2+(t)^2+(t)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{2 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\frac{y + z}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(1)[\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right)]}{t} \\  & =\frac{(1)t^2}{(1)t} \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}(t)(\sqrt{2 t^{2} + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2 t^{2} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(4 t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{3}^{5}u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{3}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[(5)^{3/2}-(3)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[(5 \sqrt{5})-(3 \sqrt{3})] \\  & =\left(\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{6}\right)-\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=6y$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t^2,t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

Use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt.
$$

For this curve, $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{4t^2+1}$. Use the substitution $u=4t^2+1$ and give the exact value.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Along the curve, $x=t^2$ and $y=t$, so $f(\mathbf r(t))=6t$. The supplied speed follows from

$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle 2t,1\rangle,\qquad
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{(2t)^2+1^2}=\sqrt{4t^2+1}.
$$

Thus

$$
\int_C 6y\,\mathrm ds=\int_0^1 6t\sqrt{4t^2+1}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

With $u=4t^2+1$, we have $\mathrm du=8t\,\mathrm dt$ and $6t\,\mathrm dt=\frac34\,\mathrm du$. Change both limits:

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $5$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C 6y\,\mathrm ds
&=\frac34\int_1^5 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\frac12\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^5\\
&=\frac{5\sqrt5-1}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral

$$
\int_C 3yz\cos x\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,\sin t,1\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le\frac\pi2.
$$

Give the exact value.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar line integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve, $x=t$, $y=\sin t$, and $z=1$. Hence

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=3\sin t\cos t.
$$

Differentiate all three coordinates and compute the speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 1,\cos t,0\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\int_C 3yz\cos x\,\mathrm ds
=\int_0^{\pi/2}3\sin t\cos t\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Choose $u=1+\cos^2t$. Then $\mathrm du=-2\sin t\cos t\,\mathrm dt$. The limits reverse:

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac\pi2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $1$ |

So

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C 3yz\cos x\,\mathrm ds
&=-\frac32\int_2^1 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\frac32\int_1^2 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^2\\
&=2\sqrt2-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The integrand is nonnegative on this interval, which also checks the sign.

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral

$$
\int_C\frac{y+z}{x}\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t,\frac{t^2}{2},t^2\right\rangle,\qquad 1\le t\le\sqrt3.
$$

Give the exact value.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar function in three variables,

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Here $x=t$, $y=t^2/2$, and $z=t^2$. Since $t\ge1$, the denominator is nonzero, and

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=\frac{t^2/2+t^2}{t}=\frac32t.
$$

All three derivative components contribute to arc length:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 1,t,2t\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{1^2+t^2+(2t)^2}=\sqrt{1+5t^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C\frac{y+z}{x}\,\mathrm ds
=\int_1^{\sqrt3}\frac32t\sqrt{1+5t^2}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Choose $u=1+5t^2$, so $\mathrm du=10t\,\mathrm dt$ and $\frac32t\,\mathrm dt=\frac3{20}\,\mathrm du$. The transformed limits are

| $t$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $6$ | $16$ |

It follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\frac{y+z}{x}\,\mathrm ds
&=\frac3{20}\int_6^{16}u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\frac1{10}\left[u^{3/2}\right]_6^{16}\\
&=\frac{64-6\sqrt6}{10}\\
&=\frac{32-3\sqrt6}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$
